en: His gold and gold coins—
Where they scattered them, I was not there.
Breaking the treasury's entrance,
O God, where they opened it, I was not there!
The white winged steed ridden for a month—
Its tail and mane I would comb—
Shall I die without braiding them?
The only child the generous one left,
Longing to see him once,
Shall I die without seeing him?
My morning star beside the moon,
My cherished Semetey,
My morning star whom I cradled!
My heir left by Manas,
My only one left by the hero,
My only one granted by fate,
O Semetey, my lamp!
Did a mighty enemy come from China
And press down upon his head?
The only child we cradled—
Did they slaughter him in sacrifice?
My companion, my child Kanykei,
My cherished lamp—
Did they make her a captive woman?
Chyiyrdy in her old age,
My cherished mother—
Did they gouge out both her eyes
And take their bitterest revenge?
Has my proudly straight back broken?
Parting me from my orphan,
Has God struck me utterly down?
Down you go, together with your camels!
Why did I turn to tending his camels?
While saying I would herd the camels,
I lost Semetey, my heart's torment.
Perish together with your livestock!
Why did I turn to tending his livestock?
While saying I would herd the livestock,
I lost Kanykei, my lively bazaar!
Alas upon alas, Semetey!
I claimed river meadows and gathered hay.
Saying I would graze my stock beside the river,
I consumed my lamp Semetey.
My dear head plunged in sorrow,
I returned to his dwelling place;
I lost my lamp Semetey.
I raided the Chinese commanders and took much.
Cursed be all that taking!
I consumed my only Semetey.
My wings were broken back;
I lost my lamp Semetey.
I blunted my steel;
I lost my valiant Kanykei.
My widow and my orphan,
I let them be taken—an evil name!
Who pledged his hand to seven patrons,
My accomplished Manas, my soul's friend,
Or else take me along with you!
A wretched beard scorched by enemies,
Is it my time to be left on the ridge?
Hiding my body broad as Keng-Kol,
How could I remain without grieving?
Semetey, left by the blood-shedder—
There is no word of where he is.
How shall I remain alive?
Hiding my body broad as Talas,
While saying I would tend the camels,
I drove my fortune away.
How shall I remain alive?
'The hoof left by the fierce wolf,' I say—
Whom shall I make my support?
Parted from my little foal Kanykei,
How shall I remain alive?
This beard enemies dared not approach,
Have you become the enemy's spoil?
This damned mustache,
Have the Chinese cut it off?
Alas upon alas, Semetey!
How can I survive you?
Devoting my blood to sacrifice,
Let me cut off my life today.
My widow and my orphan—
How can I be left parted from them?
Rather than that, my life
Let me bring to an end today!
When my friend Manas died,
I remained without dying in my place.
That I have gone on living
Was because my only Semetey was here.
Now that my beard is white,
With my final journey awaiting me,
For whom have I lamented?
That I lamented without dying
Was for the child Semetey alone.
My dark eyes worn away,
Has God struck me again?
Semetey, left by Manas—
Parting me from Semetey,
Has God struck Bakai down?
I tended camels for the sake of a life.
Not dying together with my lord,
That I have gone on just like this
Was for the child Semetey alone.
My banner fastened to a spear,
My gift left by the generous one,
Parted from my gift,
Where shall I see my only child?
Rather than go on living thus,
Alas, my orphan, let me see the face of Judgment!
Instead of remaining alive in this world,
Better that I should die!'
Plucking out his beard and casting it away,
Tearing out his mustache and casting it away,
His bellow split the stones;
His shout split heads.
The mottled-necked white blade
He took and made ready.
To turn the gray winged steed around,
To strike himself in the breast,
To cut off his precious life,
Mighty Bakai stood preparing.
His white beard had grown thin;
Bloody tears flowing from his eyes
Poured down over his collarbone.
Turning about, weeping, unable to find him,
Unable to regain his composure,
He drew out the blade.
To offer his wretched life in sacrifice,
To die this very moment,
Mighty Bakai prepared
To cut off his precious life.
Clouds parted in the sky.
His thoughts were terribly torn;
His hand hung limp,
His eyes wandered wildly.
Then he thought it over:
'If I die just now,
Will they dwell along the river?
If my Kanykei too has died,
If the child I cherished has died,
And afterward I die,
These people here—
Will they be like an extinguished fire?
My cherished Kanykei,
My daughter-in-law whom I took as companion,
My words to Allah were a lament.
Upon my child's shoulder,
Of suffering six months ahead,
There was one who could tell her now—
A naked child was there.
My dear child Kanykei
Was a soul endowed with sacred power.
She was the fairest of women.
My noble child Kanykei—
Temir Khan, who ruled Bukhara,
She was Temir Khan's daughter,
The youngest of twelve daughters,
A servant beloved of God,
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The lovely one among the Muslims—
She was a true holy woman.
Thrown into fire, she would not turn to ashes;
Fallen among enemies, she would not become a slave.
My valiant child Kanykei
Was a soul of abundant blessing.
If great suffering were to fall upon her head,
Of suffering six months ahead
She was one who knew.
Did she see that enemy?
When the thought came to Kanykei,
Did she go out into the hills?
Did she remain alive without dying?
When the thought came, did my little foal
Hide herself away?
Did they scatter her treasury and livestock?
When the thought came, did Kanykei
Flee out into the hills?
Kara-Buura and Chatkal
Let me search for two days.
Let me bear my anguish thus.
The hills of spacious Talas
Let me search for three days.
Somehow, my flower calf,
Let me find my Kanykei.'
Khan Bakai went into the hills,
Setting the gray winged steed in motion,
Calling out Kanykei's name.
On the ridges Bakai shouted,
Calling out for Kanykei.
In the hills Bakai shouted,
Calling out for Kanykei.
Down Talas he shouted,
Calling out for Chyiyrdy.
Üch-Koshoi's low, level foothills
Bakai searched for three days.
In Kara-Buura and Chatkal
He traveled for two days.
Unable to regain his composure,
Your father, old Bakai,
Tamarisk-covered Keng-Kol, the great valley—
He searched through all of it.
For Manas, gone to the other world,
Honoring the spirit of his friend,
He bore so much anguish now.
The great hills of spacious Talas
He searched without a word.
Kök-Zhaiyk at the head of Ürbüz
He searched for three days.
Through hills and steep banks,
Through caves and forests,
Leaving nothing the size of a louse,
He searched through everything.
Through every towering mountain,
Through every gaping ravine,
Leaving not a louse-sized patch,
Mighty Bakai searched thus.
Beneath him his winged steed grew weary;
His eyes grew strained, unable to see.
Not acknowledging his old age,
Bakai reproached his eyes:
'These accursed eyes
Cannot see anything at all!
Riding by night and drinking much water,
Has God struck them at the root?
These damned eyes
Cannot see a single thing!
Traveling in darkness,
Has old age stood against me?
Struck hard by snow and storms,
Has God struck their roots?
My eyes, open, do not close!
My heart, be calm, do not burn!
May what I lost be found!
Of old tiger Bakai,
May his honor thus be preserved!
Now I shall truly die.
In the desert of Kum-Bulak,
At the place where he performed ablution,
Encountered through the unseen,
Found through God's favor,
Before its eyes had opened,
He gave it milk from his mouth,
Gave it meat with his hand,
Had a steel collar fitted to its neck,
Had a tiger-skin covering laid upon its back.
'A raiding hero needs it,' he said,
And had the tiger woman Kanykei rear it.
It never drew back from a tiger,
Never turned away from a bear.
Whatever it bit, it ravaged;
Everyone who saw it, it made smile.
When dear Manas died,
It laid its head upon the ground.
At the khan's burial enclosure then,
Kumaiyk lay down howling.
Khan Manas's little enclosure—
